method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency needing empiric antibiotics without delay.** Keep a high index of suspicion in any unwell child, especially with altered mental state or no clear focus.
claims.source_text: Bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency which requires empiric antibiotic treatment without delay. A high index of suspicion for meningitis is needed in any unwell child, particularly if there is altered mental state or no clear focus of infection
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Viral and bacterial meningitis cannot be reliably told apart clinically** — treat with empiric antimicrobials until the cause is confirmed. Presentation ranges from hours to days and may be altered by recent antibiotics.
claims.source_text: Presentation of bacterial meningitis can vary from fulminant (hours) to insidious (days) and can be altered by recent treatment with antibiotics … It is difficult to distinguish viral from bacterial meningitis clinically. Children with meningitis should be treated with empiric antimicrobials until the cause is confirmed
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Meningitis and encephalitis are hard to separate but have different pathogens** — if in doubt, cover both initially.
claims.source_text: Making a clinical distinction between meningitis and encephalitis can be difficult, but is important, as the common causative pathogens differ. If there is any doubt, initial empiric management should cover both
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Infants with meningitis are often subtle:** irritability, lethargy or drowsiness, poor feeding, apnoea, vomiting and diarrhoea, temperature instability. On examination look for a full or bulging fontanelle, high-pitched cry, fever or hypothermia; **neck stiffness may be absent in infants**.
claims.source_text: subtle or non-specific symptoms irritability lethargy or drowsiness poor feeding apnoea vomiting and diarrhoea temperature instability … Full or bulging fontanelle High-pitched cry Fever or hypothermia Hyper or hypotonia Neck stiffness (may be absent in infants)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Encephalitis:** altered mental state can be subtle — unusual behaviour, confusion, personality change, emotional lability — and seizures are common. **Bradycardia and hypertension can signal raised intracranial pressure.**
claims.source_text: Features of altered mental state can be subtle and depend on the affected region of the brain: unusual behaviour confusion personality change emotional lability Seizures (common) … Bradycardia and hypertension can be signs of raised intracranial pressure
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Risk factors for meningitis:** maternal GBS colonisation (infants <3 months), unimmunised, immunocompromised, neurosurgery or penetrating head injury, VP shunt, cochlear implant, and age <5 years.
claims.source_text: Maternal group B streptococcal (GBS) colonisation in infants <3 months Unimmunised Immunocompromised (consider cryptococcus and mycobacteria) History of neurosurgery or penetrating head injury VP shunt Cochlear implant Younger age, particularly <5 years
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Urgent LP**, with urgent CSF microscopy and biochemistry, preferably with a simultaneous blood glucose.
claims.source_text: Urgent lumbar puncture (LP) … Urgent CSF microscopy and biochemistry, preferably with simultaneous blood glucose
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Defer LP and start empiric treatment immediately if it is unsafe:** focal neurological signs, ongoing seizures, markedly reduced GCS, cardiovascular compromise or coagulopathy. Do the LP as soon as a senior clinician deems it safe. Tachycardia and tachypnoea without respiratory compromise are not contraindications.
claims.source_text: If unsafe to perform (eg focal neurological signs, ongoing seizures, markedly reduced GCS, cardiovascular compromise or coagulopathy), defer LP and commence empiric treatment immediately. The LP should be performed as soon as practicable, once deemed safe by a senior clinician. Tachycardia and tachypnoea without respiratory compromise are not contraindications to lumbar puncture
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Do not delay antimicrobials in an unwell child if the LP will take more than 30 minutes.**
claims.source_text: Do not delay antimicrobials in an unwell child if the LP will take more than 30 minutes
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Bloods:** blood culture, FBE (may be normal), glucose, gas for lactate, UEC for hyponatraemia; coagulation studies if shock or coagulopathy suspected.
claims.source_text: Blood culture FBE (may be normal) Blood glucose level Blood gas for lactate UEC, assess for hyponatraemia Consider coagulation studies if shock or coagulopathy suspected
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Neuroimaging** for focal signs, raised ICP, encephalopathy or diagnostic uncertainty; not routine in meningitis. **A normal CT does not exclude raised ICP and should not drive the LP decision.**
claims.source_text: Indications include: focal neurological signs signs of raised ICP encephalopathy diagnostic uncertainty eg to look for a mass Not routine in meningitis but may be used to look for complications eg abscess, thrombosis Normal CT brain does not exclude raised ICP and should not influence the decision to perform an LP
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Cover meningitis first; add encephalitis treatment** if there is altered conscious state, focal signs, seizures, signs or risk of HSV, or the child is obtunded. **Give antibiotics within 30 minutes of the decision to treat.**
claims.source_text: Initial empiric management should cover meningitis. Treatment for encephalitis should be added if there is clinical suspicion (altered conscious state, focal neurological signs, seizures, signs or risk of HSV infection) and/or child is obtunded … Antibiotics should be given within 30 minutes of the decision to treat
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **0–2 months (GBS, E. coli, Listeria):** benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg IV — 12-hourly under 7 days old, 6–8-hourly from 7 days to <4 weeks, 4-hourly over 4 weeks — **and** cefotaxime 50 mg/kg IV — 12-hourly in week 1, 6–8-hourly from 7 days to <4 weeks, 6-hourly over 4 weeks — or ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg (max 2 g) IV daily. **Dexamethasone not advised.**
claims.source_text: 0-2 months GBS, Escherichia coli, Listeria monocytogenes (rare) Benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg IV 12 hourly (<7 days old), 6-8 hourly (7 days to <4 weeks old), 4 hourly (>4 weeks old) and Cefotaxime 50 mg/kg IV 12 hourly (week 1 of life), 6-8 hourly (7 days to <4 weeks old), 6 hourly (>4 weeks old) or Ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg (max 2 g) IV daily* Not advised
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Avoid ceftriaxone where possible in neonates <41 weeks gestation**, particularly if jaundiced or receiving calcium-containing solutions including TPN.
claims.source_text: Where possible, ceftriaxone should be avoided in neonates <41 weeks gestation, particularly if jaundiced or receiving calcium containing solutions, including TPN
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **2 months and over (N. meningitidis, S. pneumoniae, HiB):** ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg (max 4 g) IV daily **or** cefotaxime 50 mg/kg (max 2 g) IV 6-hourly. **Add vancomycin if Gram-positive cocci on Gram stain.**
claims.source_text: Ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg (max 4 g) IV daily or cefotaxime 50 mg/kg (max 2 g) IV 6 hourly Add vancomycin if Gram-positive cocci on Gram stain
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Dexamethasone (2 months and over):** 0.15 mg/kg (max 10 mg) IV 6-hourly for 4 days.
claims.source_text: N. meningitidis, S. pneumoniae, HiB Ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg (max 4 g) IV daily or cefotaxime 50 mg/kg (max 2 g) IV 6 hourly Add vancomycin if Gram-positive cocci on Gram stain (see Vancomycin for dosing) 0.15 mg/kg (max 10 mg) IV 6 hourly for 4 days
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Penicillin/cephalosporin hypersensitivity:** moxifloxacin 10 mg/kg (max 400 mg) IV daily **and** vancomycin.
claims.source_text: Penicillin/cephalosporin hypersensitivity: moxifloxacin 10 mg/kg (max 400 mg) IV daily and vancomycin
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Encephalitis — add aciclovir to the antibiotics:** 20 mg/kg IV 12-hourly (<30 weeks gestation) or 8-hourly (>30 weeks gestation to <3 months corrected age); 20 mg/kg IV 8-hourly (3 months to 12 years); 10 mg/kg IV 8-hourly (>12 years). **Consider adding azithromycin.**
claims.source_text: Aciclovir 20 mg/kg IV 12 hourly (<30 weeks gestation), 8 hourly (>30 weeks gestation to <3 months corrected age) … 20 mg/kg IV 8 hourly (3 months to 12 years) … 10 mg/kg IV 8 hourly (>12 years) Consider adding azithromycin
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Unrecognised HSV encephalitis is devastating, but early aciclovir can lead to full recovery.**
claims.source_text: Unrecognised HSV encephalitis is a devastating illness with significant morbidity and mortality, however early treatment with aciclovir can lead to a full recovery
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Steroids may reduce the risk of hearing loss** in bacterial meningitis (evidence mixed). **Not recommended in neonates** because of possible neurodevelopmental effects.
claims.source_text: Current evidence for steroids in bacterial meningitis in children is mixed, but suggests that steroids may reduce the risk of hearing loss … Steroids are not recommended in neonates due to possible effects on neurodevelopment
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Give the first IV dexamethasone just before or with the first antibiotic dose.** If given after, ideally within 4 hours and no more than 12 hours after starting antibiotics.
claims.source_text: Give the first dose of IV dexamethasone just before or with the first dose of antibiotics. If giving the first dose of IV dexamethasone after initial antibiotic administration, this should ideally be done within 4 hours and not more than 12 hours after starting antibiotics
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Treat all seizures immediately.** Resuscitate shock with **10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride IV boluses**.
claims.source_text: All seizures in the setting of meningitis or encephalitis should be treated immediately … Initial resuscitation, if required to manage shock, should be with 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride IV boluses
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Risk of excess ADH: give a maximum of 2/3 maintenance IV fluids**; further restriction may be needed for hyponatraemia or raised ICP (seek senior advice). **Always maintain normal blood pressure and adequate circulating volume.**
claims.source_text: Children with CNS infections are at higher risk of excess antidiuretic hormone (ADH) secretion and caution should be taken with ongoing fluid management. A maximum of 2/3 maintenance IV fluids should be administered as per IV fluids … Further fluid restriction may be required if there is hyponatraemia or risk of raised intracranial pressure, seek senior advice … In all children with meningitis, regardless of the presence of intracranial hypertension it is essential to ensure normal blood pressure and adequate circulating volume
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Reassess hydration, weight, sodium, acid–base and neurological state every 6–12 hours for the first 48 hours.** Droplet precautions for the first 24 hours of admission.
claims.source_text: Assessment of the clinical signs of hydration, including weight, measurement of the serum sodium and acid-base status, and clinical assessment of the neurological state should be repeated every 6-12 hours for the first 48 hours … Isolation: droplet precautions in first 24 hours of admission
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Directed durations (days):** *N. meningitidis* benzylpenicillin 7 · *S. pneumoniae* penicillin-sensitive benzylpenicillin 10 · penicillin-resistant cefotaxime/ceftriaxone (vancomycin if cephalosporin-resistant) 10 · HiB ceftriaxone/cefotaxime 10.
claims.source_text: N. meningitidis Benzylpenicillin 7 S. pneumoniae (penicillin sensitive) Benzylpenicillin 10 S. pneumoniae (penicillin resistant) Cefotaxime/ceftriaxone, Vancomycin if cephalosporin resistant 10 Haemophilus influenza B (HiB) Ceftriaxone/cefotaxime 10
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Gram-negative:** ceftriaxone/cefotaxime 21 days · **organism not isolated:** 7 days minimum · **GBS, Listeria:** benzylpenicillin 14–21 days · **HSV:** aciclovir 21 days minimum.
claims.source_text: Gram-negative Ceftriaxone/cefotaxime 21 Organism not isolated Ceftriaxone/cefotaxime 7 minimum GBS, Listeria Benzylpenicillin 14-21 HSV Aciclovir 21 minimum
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider ID consultation** for resistant organisms or immediate penicillin/cephalosporin hypersensitivity.
claims.source_text: Consider infectious diseases consultation for those with organisms resistant to first line therapy or with immediate hypersensitivity to penicillins/cephalosporins
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Notify presumed or confirmed N. meningitidis and HiB immediately**; confirmed S. pneumoniae within 5 days.
claims.source_text: All cases of presumed or confirmed N meningitidis and HiB should be notified to the Health Department immediately … Confirmed S.pneumoniae is notifiable within 5 days
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Fever persisting after 4–6 days of treatment:** consider nosocomial infection, subdural effusion or empyema, cerebral abscess or parameningeal focus, or inadequate treatment.
claims.source_text: If fever persists after 4-6 days of treatment, consider: nosocomial infection subdural effusion or empyema cerebral abscess or parameningeal focus inadequate treatment
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Transfer if** haemodynamic or respiratory instability, altered conscious state, seizures or focal signs, care beyond local comfort, or complications/poor response.
claims.source_text: Haemodynamic or respiratory instability Altered conscious state, seizures or focal neurological signs Child requiring care above the level of comfort of the local hospital Complications of meningitis or encephalitis or poor response to treatment
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **IV treatment can be completed via HITH** once haemodynamically stable, afebrile and directed treatment decided.
claims.source_text: Children can complete IV treatment through HITH services if available once haemodynamically stable, afebrile and decision made regarding directed treatment
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Hearing loss is highest after S. pneumoniae meningitis (about 22%)** and can begin within 48 hours; do baseline audiology ideally as an inpatient.
claims.source_text: S. pneumoniae meningitis has the highest risk of hearing loss (approximately 22% of cases) … Onset can occur as early as 48 hours … Audiology testing ideally should be done while still an inpatient (as a baseline)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Formal audiology 6–8 weeks after discharge for every child with encephalitis or bacterial meningitis**; monitor neurodevelopment; consider complement deficiency testing after more than one episode of meningococcal disease.
claims.source_text: All children with encephalitis or bacterial meningitis should have formal audiology assessment 6-8 weeks after discharge (earlier if concerns) … Neurodevelopmental progress should be monitored … Consider investigating for complement deficiency if the child has had >1 episode of meningococcal disease
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Meningitis and encephalitis' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Meningitis_encephalitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23
